title: The line of teachers' names
hookLine: the acknowledgments page nobody reads, and an Upanishad that stops to write one
carry: every teacher's name is part of the teaching
tomorrow: what's your lineage, the teacher asks. what if you don't know?

cards: Some books end with an acknowledgments page, and it's easy to skip: a list of people the author owes. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad has pages like that.
In the middle of its teaching it stops and says: now, the line of teachers. Then name after name. Why would a sacred text take up room with a list?

teach.b: The word is vamsha, a line.
Each name in it received the teaching from the one before: this teacher from that one, from that one, on and on. And the list doesn't stop at a well-known sage.
It climbs past the human names, and it ends with Brahman, the self-existent, and a bow: salutation to Brahman.
So one answer to why: the list is the text's way of saying this came to you by hand, through people who could have dropped it and didn't, and the source of it all is Brahman.

teach.h: THE NAMES ARE PART OF IT.
teach.b: Here's the teaching: in Hinduism the names are part of the teaching. In some lineages today, students still chant a verse honoring the whole line, from its first teacher down to their own, before they study.
Now the week, from the top. A lake, and a yaksha's question: what's the greatest wonder? A hymn that asks who really knows.
Two send-offs, and the four stages of life. Kautsa's gift, and only what he owed. Arjuna, bow fallen: teach me.
A chain back to Brahma, and a letter that hands it forward. And today, the line of teachers, written down so nobody forgets who carried it.

how: When the Brihadaranyaka is recited in full, the lines of teachers (vamsha) are chanted along with the rest; some traditions also recite their own line of gurus before study.

o: a single teacher who founds a brand-new school
a teaching that reaches you through a line of people
a family tree kept to settle who inherits land

games.q: the week at the summit. tap the pairs.
p: the line of teachers, name by name

s: the Brihadaranyaka's line of teachers stops at a well-known human sage
it climbs past the human names and ends with Brahman, the self-existent.
the Taittiriya's parting advice for hard choices is to look to the gentle and wise
act as the thoughtful, gentle people who love dharma would act.
the Gita's way to a teacher leaves no room for questions
bow, ask, serve: asking sits in the middle.

games.q: the yaksha offers one brother back. Yudhishthira chooses:
o: Nakula, so Madri has a living son too.
games.why: fairness over strength, from the start of the week. then the yaksha, Dharma, gives back all four.

practice: Count, on your fingers, the people who handed you something worth keeping: a story, a prayer, a recipe, a habit, a way of being kind. One finger for each name, slowly. If you run out of fingers, start again.

wordCard.voice: A lineage: in the Brihadaranyaka, a vamsha, a line of teachers written down name by name, back to Brahman.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a line, a lineage; the Brihadaranyaka's word for its list of teachers.

carryVoice: Your line: every teacher's name is part of the teaching. A sacred text stopped to say thank you. A week at the summit, held.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.6.1–3 (now the line of teachers: each received it from the one before; the line ends with Parameshthin from Brahman; Brahman is self-existent; salutation to Brahman); also 4.6 and 6.5

the week's texts, recalled: the Yaksha Prashna (Mahabharata, Vana Parva), Rig Veda 10.129, Taittiriya 1.11, Jabala Upanishad 4, Raghuvamsha canto 5, Bhagavad Gita 2.7 and 4.34, Mundaka 1.1.1–3, 2 Timothy 2:2
